html:
The Fall of Constantinople was the capture of the Byzantine capital by the Ottoman Turks under Sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, after a siege of 53 days. It ended the Eastern Roman Empire, the last direct heir of the Roman state.

By then the empire was little more than the city itself, cut off by Ottoman lands on both sides. Mehmed, aged 21, built a fortress on the Bosphorus to block help from the Black Sea and brought a huge army and heavy cannon, some cast by a Hungarian engineer named Orban. The defenders, led by Emperor Constantine XI, had a few thousand men, including Genoese and Venetian volunteers.

How it went:

  • The cannon pounded the ancient land walls for weeks; the defenders repaired them each night.
  • A chain blocked the harbour, the Golden Horn, so Mehmed had ships dragged overland on greased logs into it.
  • On 29 May a final assault broke through. Constantine died fighting.

Mehmed made the city his capital, and it became Istanbul, the seat of the Ottoman Empire until 1922. Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque. The Greek Orthodox Patriarch was kept on as head of the Orthodox Christians under Ottoman rule.

Western Europe was shocked but sent little help. Greek scholars who fled to Italy, some before and some after 1453, added to the Renaissance study of Greek. Some historians use 1453 to mark the end of the Middle Ages.
